prompt:
Let $a$ and $b$ be given positive coprime integers. Then for every integer $n$ there exist integers $x,y$ such that
$$n=ax+by .$$
Prove that $n=ab$ is the greatest integer for which $xy\le0$ in all such representations of $n$.
answer: For $n=ab$: $a\mid y$, $b\mid x$, so $x>0$ forces $x\ge b$ and $y\le0$. For $n>ab$: the representation with $1\le x\le b$ has $by=n-ax\ge n-ab>0$.

solutions.title: Divisibility and the smallest positive $x$
solutions.body:
**Every representation of $ab$ has $xy\le0$.** Let $ab=ax+by$. Then $a\mid by$ and $\gcd(a,b)=1$, so $a\mid y$; similarly $b\mid x$. If $x>0$ then $x\ge b$, so $by=ab-ax\le0$ and $y\le0$. If $x<0$, then $by=ab-ax>0$, so $y>0$. If $x=0$, $xy=0$. In all cases $xy\le0$.

**Every $n>ab$ has a representation with $xy>0$.** All representations of $n$ are $(x+tb,\,y-ta)$, $t\in\mathbb Z$, starting from one of them; so there is one with $1\le x\le b$. For it,
$$by=n-ax\ge n-ab>0,$$
so $y>0$ and $xy>0$.

Hence $ab$ is the greatest integer all of whose representations satisfy $xy\le0$. ∎

prompt: Prove or disprove that if a real sequence $(a_n)$ satisfies $a_{n+1}-a_n\to0$ and $a_{2n}-2a_n\to0$ as $n\to\infty$, then $a_n\to0$.

solutions.title: Telescoping over doublings
solutions.body:
**The statement is true.**

**Step 1: $a_n/n\to0$.** Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $N$ with $|a_{k+1}-a_k|<\varepsilon$ for $k\ge N$. Then $|a_n|\le|a_N|+(n-N)\varepsilon$ for $n\ge N$, so $\limsup|a_n|/n\le\varepsilon$. (This is the Stolz–Cesàro lemma.)

**Step 2.** Let $C_N=\sup_{m\ge N}|a_{2m}-2a_m|$; then $C_N\to0$ because $a_{2m}-2a_m\to0$. For $n\ge N$ and $K\ge0$ we have the telescoping identity
$$\frac{a_n}n-\frac{a_{n2^{K+1}}}{n2^{K+1}}=\sum_{k=0}^K\left(\frac{a_{n2^k}}{n2^k}-\frac{a_{n2^{k+1}}}{n2^{k+1}}\right)=\sum_{k=0}^K\frac{2a_{n2^k}-a_{n2^{k+1}}}{n2^{k+1}} .$$
Every index $n2^k\ge N$, so each term has absolute value at most $\frac{C_N}{n2^{k+1}}$. Letting $K\to\infty$ and using Step 1 for the second term on the left,
$$\left|\frac{a_n}n\right|\le\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{C_N}{n2^{k+1}}=\frac{C_N}n,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad |a_n|\le C_N\ \text{ for all } n\ge N .$$
Since $C_N\to0$, $a_n\to0$. ∎

(The first hypothesis is needed: $a_n=n$ satisfies $a_{2n}-2a_n=0$ but not $a_{n+1}-a_n\to0$.)

solutions.title: Boundedness and accumulation points
solutions.body:
Steps 1 and 2 of the first solution with $N=1$ show that $(a_n)$ is bounded: $|a_n|\le C_1=\sup_m|a_{2m}-2a_m|<\infty$.

Suppose $a_n\not\to0$. By Bolzano–Weierstrass there is a subsequence $a_{n_j}\to a\ne0$. Then $a_{2n_j}=2a_{n_j}+(a_{2n_j}-2a_{n_j})\to2a$, and inductively $a_{2^sn_j}\to2^sa$ for every $s\ge1$. So $2^sa$ is an accumulation point of $(a_n)$ for every $s$, and $|2^sa|\to\infty$, contradicting boundedness. Hence $a_n\to0$. ∎

prompt:
Let $A$ and $B$ be two $n\times n$ matrices with integer entries such that all of the matrices
$$A,\quad A+B,\quad A+2B,\quad A+3B,\quad\dots,\quad A+(2n)B$$
are invertible and their inverses have integer entries, too. Show that $A+(2n+1)B$ is also invertible and that its inverse has integer entries.
answer: $P(t)=\det(A+tB)$ is a polynomial of degree $\le n$ taking values $\pm1$ at the $2n+1$ points $0,\dots,2n$; one value is taken $n+1$ times, so $P$ is constant $\pm1$; then the adjugate formula gives an integer inverse.

solutions.title: A determinant polynomial
solutions.body:
If an integer matrix $M$ has an integer inverse, then $\det M\cdot\det M^{-1}=1$ with both factors integers, so $\det M=\pm1$. Conversely, if $M$ is an integer matrix with $\det M=\pm1$, then $M^{-1}=\frac{1}{\det M}\operatorname{adj}M$ has integer entries (the adjugate consists of cofactors, which are integers).

Let $P(t)=\det(A+tB)$. Expanding the determinant, $P$ is a polynomial in $t$ of degree at most $n$ (with integer coefficients). By the first remark, $P(t)\in\{1,-1\}$ for $t=0,1,\dots,2n$. These are $2n+1$ points, so by pigeonhole one of the values, say $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$, is taken at least $n+1$ times. Then $P(t)-\varepsilon$ has degree at most $n$ and at least $n+1$ roots, so $P\equiv\varepsilon$.

In particular $\det\big(A+(2n+1)B\big)=\varepsilon=\pm1$, so $A+(2n+1)B$ is invertible and, by the second remark, its inverse has integer entries. ∎

prompt:
Let $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be a function satisfying
$$|f(x)-f(y)|\le|x-y|$$
for every $x,y\in[0,1]$. Show that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists a countable family of rectangles $(R_i)$ of dimensions $a_i\times b_i$, $a_i\le b_i$, in the plane such that
$$\{(x,f(x)) : x\in[0,1]\}\subset\bigcup_iR_i\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sum_ia_i<\varepsilon .$$
(The edges of the rectangles are not necessarily parallel to the coordinate axes.)
answer: Call $[x,y]$ *$\eta$-flat* if the graph over it stays within $\eta(y-x)$ of the chord; any non-flat interval contains a subinterval of proportional length whose slope is larger by $\eta$, so after at most $1/\eta$ steps one finds a flat subinterval of length $\ge c|I|$. Exhaust $[0,1]$ by flat intervals (thin rectangles along chords, total width $\le2\eta$) up to a remainder of small length (covered by small squares).

solutions.title: Flat pieces along chords
solutions.body:
Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and put $\eta=\varepsilon/4$ (we may assume $\varepsilon<1$). For an interval $I=[x,y]$ with $x<y$ let $\ell_I$ be the linear function with $\ell_I(x)=f(x)$, $\ell_I(y)=f(y)$, let its slope be $s(I)=\frac{f(y)-f(x)}{y-x}$, so $|s(I)|\le1$, and call $I$ **flat** if $|f(z)-\ell_I(z)|\le\eta\,(y-x)$ for all $z\in I$.

**Lemma 1.** If $I=[x,y]$ is not flat, it contains a subinterval $I'$ with $|I'|>\eta|I|$ and $|s(I')|\ge|s(I)|+\eta$.

*Proof.* Replacing $f$ by $-f$ if necessary we may assume $s=s(I)\ge0$. Take $z\in(x,y)$ with $|f(z)-\ell_I(z)|>\eta(y-x)$.
- If $f(z)>\ell_I(z)+\eta(y-x)$, let $I'=[x,z]$. Then $f(z)-f(x)>s(z-x)+\eta(y-x)$, so $s(I')>s+\eta\frac{y-x}{z-x}\ge s+\eta$. Since $f(z)-f(x)\le z-x$, we get $(z-x)(1-s)>\eta(y-x)$, hence $z-x>\eta(y-x)$.
- If $f(z)<\ell_I(z)-\eta(y-x)$, let $I'=[z,y]$. Then $f(y)-f(z)>s(y-z)+\eta(y-x)$, and the same two estimates give $s(I')>s+\eta$ and $y-z>\eta(y-x)$. $\square$

**Lemma 2.** With $c=\eta^{\lfloor1/\eta\rfloor}>0$, every interval $I$ of positive length contains a flat subinterval of length at least $c|I|$.

*Proof.* Starting from $I_0=I$, apply Lemma 1 as long as the current interval is not flat. After $j$ steps $|s(I_j)|\ge j\eta$, and $|s|\le1$, so the process stops after some $j\le\lfloor 1/\eta\rfloor$ steps at a flat $I_j$ with $|I_j|>\eta^j|I|\ge c|I|$. $\square$

**Rectangles for flat intervals.** If $C=[x,y]$ is flat, let $L=\sqrt{(y-x)^2+(f(y)-f(x))^2}$ be the length of the chord and use coordinates $(t,u)$ along and perpendicular to the chord, with origin at $(x,f(x))$. A point $(z,f(z))$, $z\in C$, equals $(z,\ell_C(z))+(0,\delta)$ with $|\delta|\le\eta|C|$; the first point has $t\in[0,L]$, $u=0$, and adding $(0,\delta)$ changes $t$ and $u$ by at most $|\delta|$. So the graph over $C$ lies in the rectangle $t\in[-\eta|C|,L+\eta|C|]$, $u\in[-\eta|C|,\eta|C|]$, of dimensions $a\times b$ with $a=2\eta|C|\le b=L+2\eta|C|$.

**Exhaustion.** Start with the family $\mathcal G_0=\{[0,1]\}$ of "gaps". Given a finite family $\mathcal G_s$ of non-overlapping closed intervals, in each $J\in\mathcal G_s$ of positive length choose by Lemma 2 a flat $C_J\subseteq J$ with $|C_J|\ge c|J|$; removing the interior of $C_J$ leaves at most two closed intervals of total length $\le(1-c)|J|$. These, together with the intervals of length $0$ in $\mathcal G_s$ (kept unchanged), form $\mathcal G_{s+1}$. The total length of $\mathcal G_s$ is at most $(1-c)^s$; fix $s$ with $(1-c)^s<\varepsilon/4$. The flat intervals chosen in steps $0,\dots,s-1$ have disjoint interiors, and together with the intervals of $\mathcal G_s$ they cover $[0,1]$.

- Each flat interval $C$ gets the rectangle above; their widths sum to $\sum2\eta|C|\le2\eta=\varepsilon/2$.
- $\mathcal G_s$ has at most $2^s$ intervals. Over $J\in\mathcal G_s$ the values of $f$ lie in an interval of length $\le|J|$ (as $f$ is $1$-Lipschitz), so the graph over $J$ lies in an axis-parallel square of side $|J|+\varepsilon 2^{-s-2}$. These widths sum to less than $\varepsilon/4+2^s\cdot\varepsilon2^{-s-2}=\varepsilon/2$.

Altogether finitely many rectangles with $a_i\le b_i$ cover the graph and $\sum a_i<\varepsilon$. ∎
